title: Primary pituitary tuberculosis
case_text:
A 50-year-old woman presented to the neurosurgery outpatient department complaining of progressively increasing headache, and diminished vision for 1 year. On physical examination, the patient was conscious and oriented. There was no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, edema or lymphadenopathy on clinical examination. Her weight and height were 164 cm and 72 kg respectively. Her Glasgow coma score was 15 (E4V5M6). The lungs examination was clear on auscultation. The patient was hypertensive on medication. The routine laboratory workup showed hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dl (reference range [RR]; 14g/dl - 16g/dl), leukocytes 8300/mm3 (RR; 4000 - 11000/mm3), and platelets 2.2x105/mm3 (RR; 1.5x105- 4.5x105/ mm3). ESR was 40 mm in the first hour. The biochemical examination showed prolactin level of 58.00 ng/ml (RR; 2.1 - 17.7 ng/ml), luteinizing hormone <0.216mIU/ml (RR; 1.5 - 9.3 mIU/ml), follicle-stimulating hormone 3.07 mIU/ml (RR; 1.4 - 18.1 mIU/ml), serum cortisol 2.27 ng/ml (RR; 4.30 - 22.0 microg/dl), thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.2microIU/ml (RR; 0.35 - 5.5 IU/ml), T3 - 0.96 ng/dl (RR; 0.6 - 1.65 ng/ml), and T4 - 4.30 microg/dl (RR; 4.4 -11 microg/dl). The serum electrolytes were within normal limits. Her chest X-ray revealed normal lung parenchyma. There was no family or close contact history with tuberculosis. No evidence of extrapulmonary lesion that could raise the suspicion of tuberculosis was noted. The contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan revealed enhancing mass lesion of 1.7 x 1.4 cm arising from the sella, causing compression of optic chiasma (Figure 11B).
A radiological diagnosis of pituitary macroadenoma was given, and the patient was submitted to a transsphenoidal endonasal tumor excision. The postoperative period was uneventful. The histopathology showed numerous epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells with a mixed and variable proportion of pituitary parenchymal cells arranged in a nested and alveolar pattern (Figure 222C). Reticulin stain demonstrated reticulin fibers around the nest of viable pituitary parenchymal cells (Figure 2D). Ziehl Neelsen staining demonstrated acid-fast bacilli (Figure 3).
Based on the above histomorphology, a diagnosis of Pituitary tuberculoma was given. Suspicion of pituitary adenoma was ruled out by the reticulin stain, and the demonstration of acid-fast bacilli by Ziehl Nelson stain. Treatment for tuberculosis was initiated with a 2-month combination of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 7 months of isoniazid and rifampicin. Her headache rapidly resolved and restored normal vision. Her hormone levels returned to normal after 2 months of follow-up. The outcome was uneventful and the patient is doing well after 15 months of follow-up.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: primary pituitary tuberculoma mimicking pituitary macroadenoma
